findings.finding: Benton Facial Recognition Test 42/54 (normal range): matching of unfamiliar faces across views is preserved. Object recognition 100% correct.

Famous Faces Test (East Asian public figures): 9/30 identified (below the 5th percentile), with loss of biographical knowledge even when the name is given. Family photographs: 5/8 personally known people identified, relying on contextual cues (uniform, setting) rather than the face.
Interpersonal Reactivity Index, empathic concern (son): 4/28, severely reduced. NPI-Q: apathy/indifference 6/12, disinhibition 0/12, aberrant motor behaviour (rituals) 6/12.
Frontal Behavioral Inventory (informant) 26/72: elevated on apathy (7/12), perseveration (8/12) and personal neglect (6/12); verbal disinhibition low (2/12).
D-KEFS Trail Making switching 8th percentile; Color-Word inhibition 12th percentile: moderately impaired.

Boston Naming Test 49/60 (25th percentile, low average) without semantic errors; single-word comprehension intact; fluent speech, intact grammar, no paraphasias; no surface dyslexia; category fluency (animals) 11 in 60 s (20th percentile).
HVLT-R immediate recall 9/12 (35th percentile), delayed recall 7/12 (30th percentile), recognition 11/12 (55th percentile): mild retrieval weakness with preserved recognition.
Rey-Osterrieth figure copy 32/36 (60th percentile); WAIS-IV block design scaled score 9 (37th percentile): no visuospatial deficit.

output.impression: 1. Severe loss of familiar-face identification and person-specific knowledge with preserved face perception, object recognition and visuospatial function: an associative (multimodal person-knowledge) deficit rather than a perceptual one. 2. Markedly reduced empathy and moderate executive impairment on informant and test measures. 3. Naming, single-word comprehension and recognition memory relatively preserved. The profile is consistent with right anterior temporal-predominant dysfunction.

output.query: right temporal variant frontotemporal dementia and prosopagnosia

results.finding: The right temporal variant presents with loss of familiar-face and person knowledge, behavioural change with loss of empathy, rigidity and compulsions, and episodic memory complaints; imaging shows right-predominant anterior temporal atrophy.
results.source: Ulugut Erkoyun H et al. A clinical-radiological framework of the right temporal variant of frontotemporal dementia. Brain 2020;143:2831-2843

results.finding: Right temporal lobe atrophy is associated with prosopagnosia, behavioural change and memory complaints, and is often first assessed in ophthalmology or psychiatry.
results.source: Chan D et al. The clinical profile of right temporal lobe atrophy. Brain 2009;132:1287-1298

results.finding: Behavioural features are scored against the six core features regardless of the predominant atrophy side.
results.source: Rascovsky K et al. Brain 2011;134:2456-2477 (FTDC criteria for bvFTD)

output.summary: Right-predominant anterior temporal degeneration presents with loss of familiar-face and person knowledge together with behavioural change, and is often first seen in ophthalmology or psychiatry. The face-recognition deficit is associative, with preserved face perception, in contrast to the apperceptive prosopagnosia of occipitotemporal lesions.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Apathy, loss of empathy and stereotyped routines on the family's history, with loss of familiar-face and person recognition and no depressive symptoms; MoCA 20/30
action_criteria.label: Structured informant history and bedside cognitive screen scored against the Rascovsky features
action_criteria.rationale: The behavioural features come from her son and daughter-in-law; the assessment also documents the face and person recognition loss and the absence of depressive symptoms.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe loss of familiar-face and person knowledge with preserved face perception and visuospatial function; markedly reduced empathy; moderate executive impairment
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological battery including face and person recognition, executive and social-cognition measures
action_criteria.rationale: Separates an associative loss of person knowledge from a perceptual face deficit and quantifies the empathy and executive profile.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal blood count, chemistry, thyroid function, B12, folate and inflammatory markers
action_criteria.label: Reversible-cause blood tests: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, ESR, CRP
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory contributors before attributing decline to neurodegeneration.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe right-predominant anterior temporal and amygdala atrophy with posterior cortex sparing
action_criteria.label: MRI brain without contrast, dementia protocol
action_criteria.rationale: Shows whether the anterior temporal atrophy is right-predominant, which explains the person-recognition loss, and excludes a structural or vascular cause.

action_criteria.label: FDG-PET when the structural picture is unresolved
action_criteria.rationale: Frontal and anterior temporal hypometabolism with posterior sparing supports FTD over AD.

action_criteria.rationale: Onset about 62 without a suggestive family history: the FTD consortium advises C9orf72 screening in possible or probable bvFTD, UK eligibility does not, so a counselled panel is optional.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not refer for primary ophthalmologic workup (retina, visual cortex, refraction) as the sole evaluation for the face-recognition complaint: the ophthalmology evaluation is already documented as normal, and the deficit is an associative agnosia, not a perceptual disorder.
Do not continue or escalate antidepressant therapy as the primary treatment for behavioral symptoms without completing the dementia workup: treating FTD apathy as depression delays diagnosis.
Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
required_recommendations: Apply the Rascovsky 2011 criteria: state the features present (apathy, loss of empathy, stereotyped routines), the functional decline, and the level of certainty (probable, given the right anterior temporal atrophy), and name the right temporal presentation (loss of familiar-face and person knowledge).

Explain that the face-recognition failure is an associative loss of person knowledge from right anterior temporal degeneration, not a visual disorder, so no further ophthalmological work-up is needed.

Explain why depression does not account for the syndrome: no low mood, hopelessness, guilt or appetite change, no response to sertraline, and progressive behavioural change with anterior temporal atrophy.
Address safety and capacity: driving, finances, and her vulnerability because she cannot tell familiar people from strangers.

Arrange caregiver education and support for her son and daughter-in-law, and a behavioural plan for the rigid routines; review the antidepressant against its effect on the compulsive behaviour rather than escalating it for depression, and avoid cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise anterior temporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; no parkinsonism is present. Not indicated in this case.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not part of the FTD work-up; FDG-PET or perfusion SPECT is the functional study when one is needed.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.

differential.key_features: Shares anterior temporal degeneration; against it: right-predominant atrophy, language is not the leading deficit, single-word comprehension intact, naming low average without semantic errors.

Bedside recall and orientation loss and mild right hippocampal atrophy raise it; against it: preserved recognition memory and posterior cortex and an anterior temporal pattern. An amyloid or CSF AD biomarker study is optional if doubt remains.
Against: no subjective low mood, hopelessness, guilt or appetite change, no response to sertraline, progressive prosopagnosia and anterior temporal atrophy (Ducharme 2020).
Fazekas grade 1 only; no infarct; the lobar anterior temporal pattern is degenerative.
Normal ophthalmology, acuity 20/25, full fields, intact object recognition and face perception.

key_clinical_evidence: Apathy, loss of empathy and rigid routines on the family's history with loss of familiar-face and person knowledge, no depressive symptoms and no response to sertraline.

Neuropsychology: severe loss of famous and familiar face identification and person knowledge with normal face perception (Benton) and visuospatial function, an associative rather than perceptual deficit; markedly reduced empathy.
MRI: severe right-predominant anterior temporal and amygdala atrophy with posterior cortex sparing: imaging support for probable bvFTD with a right temporal presentation.
The anterior temporal pattern with relative posterior sparing makes Alzheimer disease less likely; an amyloid or CSF AD biomarker study is optional if doubt remains.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The face-recognition failure is associative agnosia from right anterior temporal degeneration, not a primary visual deficit. Visual acuity, fields, and extraocular movements are normal on neurological exam; object recognition and visuospatial function are intact. The ophthalmology evaluation is appropriately unremarkable.
red_herrings.data_point: Family initially brought patient to ophthalmology for 'vision problem' and ophthalmology found no primary ocular pathology
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could anchor the diagnostic workup on primary visual or ophthalmologic causes, prompting repeat visual field testing, OCT, or neuro-ophthalmology referral instead of dementia evaluation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Apathy in FTD is not depression: the patient lacks subjective dysphoria, hopelessness, and neurovegetative features; behavioral symptoms including stereotypy, empathy loss, and prosopagnosia are not features of depression and do not respond to antidepressants. Progressive neuroimaging findings are incompatible with primary mood disorder.
red_herrings.data_point: Prior psychiatric diagnosis of major depressive disorder and ongoing sertraline 50 mg initiated 3 months ago
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could mislead the clinician into attributing all behavioral changes (apathy, social withdrawal, loss of interest) to undertreated or treatment-resistant depression, leading to antidepressant escalation rather than dementia evaluation.

results.finding: Three of six core features within the first three years define possible bvFTD. Probable bvFTD requires functional decline and supportive imaging.

results.finding: New mid-life behavioural change with functional decline warrants a neurodegenerative work-up.
results.source: Ducharme S et al. Recommendations to distinguish bvFTD from psychiatric disorders. Brain 2020;143:1632-1650

behavioural variant frontotemporal demen.summary: Rascovsky and colleagues (2011) define possible behavioural variant FTD by three of six behavioural and cognitive features, probable bvFTD by added functional decline and frontal or anterior temporal involvement on structural or functional imaging, and definite bvFTD by histopathology or a pathogenic mutation. New behavioural change in mid-life with progressive functional decline should prompt a neurodegenerative work-up even in a person with a psychiatric history. Treatment is supportive: SSRIs or trazodone for behaviour, caregiver support and safety planning; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not recommended.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured behavioural/cognitive assessment with informant, validated neuropsychological testing, targeted baseline labs, and brain MRI. Case-specific additions: optional FDG-PET.
metadata.notes: Right temporal-predominant bvFTD. Cardinal feature: associative loss of familiar-face and person knowledge from right anterior temporal degeneration, with apathy, loss of empathy and rigid routines. Teaching: laterality (right anterior temporal atrophy explains the person-recognition loss), the depression trap, and prosopagnosia localisation. Two red herrings: the ophthalmology referral and the depression diagnosis.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. L is a 64-year-old right-handed retired East Asian accountant brought to the neurology clinic by her son and daughter-in-law after a 2-year course of gradually progressive behavioral change and loss of face and person recognition. The family's initial concern was her repeated failure to recognise the faces of neighbors, family friends, and even briefly-disguised family members (e.g., son arriving with a beard), which they interpreted as a vision problem. She was referred to ophthalmology 6 months ago, where visual acuity, fields, and eye movement examination were normal and no primary ocular pathology was found. Despite reassurance, face-recognition failure has continued and the family has now noted additional features: she can no longer recall the personal histories of people she knew well: she does not remember that her neighbor Mrs. Park lost her husband last year, that a close friend relocated, or any biographic facts about colleagues she worked alongside for decades. She describes these individuals as 'unfamiliar' even when told their names. In contrast, she still recognises common objects and familiar places. Object naming, basic word-finding in conversation, and reading remain intact. Concurrent personality change has been progressive in a formerly warm, socially engaged woman: she has become emotionally flat and unresponsive to family distress, did not comfort her daughter-in-law during a bereavement, and seems indifferent to the death of a close friend. She has developed rigid daily routines, eating congee at exactly the same time every morning and watching the same three television programs in sequence each day, and becomes visibly agitated if the routine is disrupted. She has lost interest in gardening and mahjong with friends, which she formerly enjoyed. Her appetite is unchanged. These behavioral features prompted a psychiatric evaluation 4 months ago, resulting in a diagnosis of major depression (attributed to widowhood; her husband died 3 years ago) and initiation of sertraline 50 mg. After 3 months, behavioral symptoms and face-recognition failure have not improved. She herself does not endorse depressed mood, hopelessness, guilt, or anhedonia beyond routine preferences; she lacks insight into her cognitive or social difficulties. Past medical history includes well-controlled hypertension, osteopenia, and mild hyperlipidemia. No family history of dementia. Never smoked. No significant alcohol use. Medications: losartan 50 mg, rosuvastatin 10 mg, calcium/vitamin D, sertraline 50 mg (initiated 3 months ago). Allergy: penicillin (rash).

neurological_exam.additional: History from her son and daughter-in-law. She navigated the clinic independently and read the consent form without difficulty. No apraxia, neglect or visual inattention.
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact finger-nose, heel-shin. Normal rapid alternating movements bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Visual acuity 20/25 bilaterally with current spectacles. Visual fields: full to confrontation bilaterally. Extraocular movements: full, no nystagmus. Pupils: equal, round, reactive bilaterally. Facial sensation intact. Facial strength symmetric. Hearing intact to finger rub bilaterally. No dysarthria.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal cadence, stride, and arm swing. No parkinsonian features. Tandem gait intact.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Cooperative. Speaks fluent, grammatically intact English and Mandarin (per family). On informal bedside testing with family photographs she cannot identify her son's work colleagues whom she has met repeatedly over 5 years; shown a photograph of a former colleague, Mr. Chen, she describes 'a middle-aged man' but cannot recall who he is. She recognises familiar objects normally, identifies basic geometric shapes and reads printed words without difficulty.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone. Strength 5/5 throughout all extremities, bilateral and symmetric. No tremor. No rigidity. No fasciculations. No alien-limb phenomenon. No apraxia of either hand.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric throughout all extremities. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. Bilateral palmomental reflexes present. Snout reflex present. Grasp reflex absent.
neurological_exam.sensory: Normal to light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception bilaterally. No cortical sensory loss. No extinction to double simultaneous stimulation.
